name: Andrew Johnson
role: President of the United States (1865–1869); earlier Tennessee legislator, governor and senator
summary: Andrew Johnson combined Unionism and support for small homesteaders with strong states’ rights and opposition to federal Reconstruction. He resisted Black political equality, defended presidential authority against Congress, and proposed direct elections and a single presidential term.

sources.title: State of the Union Addresses, 1865–1868
sources.author: Andrew Johnson, Project Gutenberg
sources.usedFor: Full collection downloaded and searched: Union, religious separation, homesteads, economy and constitutional government.

sources.title: Civil Rights bill veto, March 27, 1866
sources.author: Andrew Johnson, Miller Center
sources.usedFor: Full text downloaded: citizenship, racial distinctions, interracial marriage and federal enforcement.

sources.title: Freedmen’s Bureau veto, February 19, 1866
sources.author: Andrew Johnson, Miller Center
sources.usedFor: Full text downloaded: relief, dependency, education, property and military jurisdiction.

sources.title: Special Message, July 18, 1868: proposed constitutional amendments
sources.author: Andrew Johnson, American Presidency Project
sources.usedFor: Full text downloaded: direct executive and Senate elections, one presidential term and judicial tenure.

sources.title: Tenure of Office bill veto, March 2, 1867
sources.author: Andrew Johnson, American Presidency Project
sources.usedFor: Personal argument for executive removal authority, independent departments and presidential responsibilities.

sources.title: Third Annual Message, December 3, 1867
sources.author: Andrew Johnson, Miller Center
sources.usedFor: Racial exclusion, military reconstruction, constitutional means and racial-government arguments; also read in full collection.

sources.title: Fourth Annual Message, December 1868
sources.author: Andrew Johnson, Miller Center
sources.usedFor: Debt, banks, peacetime military cuts, Indigenous reservations, peaceful expansion and institutional reform; also searched in downloaded collection. Host and Gutenberg dates differ.

sources.title: Andrew Johnson
sources.author: Paul H. Bergeron, Tennessee Encyclopedia
sources.usedFor: Complete career from tailor and legislator through military governorship, presidency and 1875 Senate return.

sources.title: Andrew Johnson, the Freedmen’s Bureau, and the Problem of Equal Rights, 1865–1866
sources.author: Donald G. Nieman, Journal of Southern History 44 (1978), 399–420
sources.usedFor: Downloaded searchable article; legal protection and Johnson’s personal obstruction of expanded Bureau jurisdiction.

sources.title: Andrew Johnson and Reconstruction
sources.author: National Park Service
sources.usedFor: Property restoration, amnesty and distinction between Johnson’s and congressional programs.

sources.title: Andrew Johnson

sources.title: Andrew Johnson: Domestic Affairs

sources.title: Andrew Johnson: Foreign Affairs

notes: No inferred answers. Four complete annual messages, civil-rights and relief vetoes and the full constitutional-reform proposal were downloaded and searched across themes. The whole 490-statement list and remaining unknowns were reviewed. Earlier proslavery identification is not treated as his mature support for continued slavery: he helped abolish it, while rejecting racial political equality. Claims of universal natural rights are retained alongside his contrary racial positions at low confidence. Wartime suppression and later attacks on military Reconstruction are distinguished, rather than assuming either an unconditional libertarian or an unconditional repression position. Judicial term limits are not conflated with recallable judges. A single presidential term does not establish term limits for every office. Specie redemption does not imply abolition of central banking, and criticism of interest and bank privilege does not imply banning all interest. Peaceful expansion is supported by his own 1868 advocacy, not merely assent to Seward’s Alaska purchase. Neither general racial prejudice nor claims of governmental incapacity establish genetic causation. Reservations establish relocation policy, not authority of tribes over every traditional territory. Consent for a proposed island purchase does not address disputed-territory plebiscites. A promise to honor treaty rights does not by itself establish the specific rule that alteration always requires both parties’ agreement. No modern climate, technology, sexual-law or women’s-suffrage position assigned without evidence. The 1875 return to the Senate was reviewed for chronology; no later repudiation of these substantive positions was found.
